replacement: “Yes, life is full. There’s life even underground,” he started again. “You won’t believe it, Alexey, but how I want to live now! Inside these peeling walls a hunger for existence and awareness has come over me. Rakitin can’t grasp that. All he wants is to build a house and rent out apartments. But you, I’ve been longing for you. And what is suffering anyway? I’m not afraid of it, even if there were no end to it. I’m not afraid of it now. I was before. Do you know, maybe I won’t answer at the trial at all.... And I seem to have such strength in me now that I think I could bear anything, any pain at all, as long as I can say it to myself every moment: ‘I exist.’ In a thousand agonies—I exist. Stretched on the rack—I exist! Though I sit alone on top of a pillar—I exist! I see the sun, and if I can’t see the sun, I know it’s there. And a whole life lies in that, in knowing the sun is there. Alyosha, my angel, all these philosophies are the death of me. Damn them! Brother Ivan—”
“Who? You mean that fairy tale about the crazy idiot, the epileptic, Smerdyakov?”
“No, Ivan. You have told yourself several times that you are the murderer.”

But Ivan did not answer. Alyosha stood under the lamp-post at the crossroads until Ivan had disappeared into the dark. Then he turned and walked slowly home. Both Alyosha and Ivan lived in lodgings, since neither would live in Fyodor Pavlovitch’s empty house. Alyosha rented a furnished room from some working people. Ivan lived some distance off. He had taken a roomy, fairly comfortable lodge attached to a fine house, owned by a well-to-do lady, an official’s widow. His only servant was a deaf, rheumatic old crone who went to bed at six every evening and rose at six every morning. Ivan had lately become remarkably careless of comfort, and very fond of solitude. He did everything for himself in the single room he lived in, and he seldom set foot in any other room of the lodge.
